--- toc-title: In this lesson --- # 15 Clipping In this lesson we will learn how to clip different geometries. By the end of this lesson, students will be able to: - reproject geo-dataframes so they share the same CRS before combining them - clip a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` to the polygons of another one using `geopandas.clip()` - subset tabular data before applying geospatial operations - clip a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` to a bounding box using `total_bounds` - decide when to clip to a bounding box instead of the exact polygons ## About the data We will use three datasets in this lesson. The first dataset is a [TIGER shapefile of the US states from the United States Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-line-file.2026.html#form-dropdown-790442341) @us_census_bureau_tiger_2026. [TIGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topologically_Integrated_Geographic_Encoding_and_Referencing) stands for Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing. TIGER is the US Census Bureau's geographic database, and TIGER/Line files are extracts from it. Earlier versions of these files used a plain-text (ASCII) format; beginning with the 2007 version, they are distributed as shapefiles. You can view the metadata for all the TIGER shapefiles [here](https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/data/tiger/tgrshp2026/TGRSHP2026_TechDoc.pdf). Follow these steps to download the shapefile with the United States' states: 1. At the [2026 TIGER page](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-line-file.2026.html#form-dropdown-790442341), under Download, click on "Web Interface". 2. For year, select 2026, and for layer type select "States (and equivalent)". Click submit. 3. Click on "Download national file". The column descriptions for the US states shapefile, from the [TIGER/Line Shapefiles technical documentation](https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/data/tiger/tgrshp2026/TGRSHP2026_TechDoc.pdf), are: | Column | Type | Description | |--------|------|-------------| | `REGION` | String | Region code | | `DIVISION` | String | Division code | | `STATEFP` | String | State FIPS code | | `STATENS` | String | State NS code | | `GEOID` | String | State identifier; state FIPS code | | `GEOIDFQ` | String | Fully qualified GEOID; used to join data tables from data.census.gov | | `STUSPS` | String | Two-character United States Postal Service (USPS) state postal abbreviation | | `NAME` | String | State name | | `LSAD` | String | LSAD code for the state | | `MTFCC` | String | MAF/TIGER Feature Class Code (G4000) | | `FUNCSTAT` | String | Functional status | | `ALAND` | Number | Land area | | `AWATER` | Number | Water area | | `INTPTLAT` | String | Latitude of the internal point | | `INTPTLON` | String | Longitude of the internal point | The second dataset we'll use is [Natural Earth's simple medium scale populated places dataset](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/downloads/50m-cultural-vectors/) @natural_earth_populated_places_50m. We can obtain this dataset by downloading the shapefile (choose the one that says "simple (less columns)"). The third dataset we'll use is [Natural Earth's road dataset](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/downloads/10m-cultural-vectors/roads/) @natural_earth_roads_10m. We can obtain this dataset by downloading the shapefile. We will combine these datasets to create the following map of infrastructure in Alaska: ![](/book/images/lesson-13/alaska.png) For these notes, all the data is inside a `data/` directory at the same level as the notebook. ## Import data Let's start by loading our libraries and then importing the datasets we will use. ::: {#71d99620 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import geopandas as gpd pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None) # ------------------------------------- # Import states polygons states = gpd.read_file(os.path.join('data', 'tl_2026_us_state', 'tl_2026_us_state.shp') ) # Import Natural Earth populated places points places = gpd.read_file(os.path.join('data', 'ne_50m_populated_places_simple', 'ne_50m_populated_places_simple.shp') ) # Import roads lines roads = gpd.read_file(os.path.join('data', 'ne_10m_roads', 'ne_10m_roads.shp') ) ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in Use a `for` loop to iterate over the three geo-dataframes we imported and change their column names to lowercase. ::: ## Prepare Alaska multipolygon Let's take a look at our `states` geo-dataframe. Since this is a geospatial dataset, exploration should include *at least* checking the head of the dataset, plotting the data, and looking at its CRS. ::: {#eefcae52 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"CRS: {states.crs}") states.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CRS: EPSG:4269 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=190} ```{=html}

This happens because the westernmost Aleutian Islands cross the 180° meridian (the *antimeridian*): their longitudes jump from -180° to about +172°, so they are drawn on the opposite side of the plot. To fix this, we will reproject the Alaska geo-dataframe to the EPSG:3338 CRS. This CRS is a *projected* CRS, better suited for working with data from Alaska: ![Source: [spatialreference.org](https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/3338/)](/book/images/lesson-13/epsg_3338.png) ::: {#5a385e2a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Reproject to CRS optimized for Alaska alaska = alaska.to_crs('epsg:3338') # Inspect the new CRS print('Is this CRS projected? ', alaska.crs.is_projected) alaska.crs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Is this CRS projected? Remember this is the EPSG code for the WGS 84 CRS. This is not a surprise since the places data is global and EPSG:4326/WGS 84 is the most widely used CRS for such data. Let's see what happens when we try to plot this data on top of Alaska: ::: {#71cf103b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Trouble fig, ax = plt.subplots() alaska.plot(ax=ax) places.plot(ax=ax, color='red') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=571 height=413} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Data in weird places? Check your CRSs This is a classic slip in geospatial analysis. To plot, analyze, or integrate different geospatial datasets they **must have the same CRS**. Here, `alaska` and `places` have different CRSs, leading to unexpected results when plotting them together: ::: {#b253af34 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} alaska.crs == places.crs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=198} ``` False ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in Reproject the `places` geo-dataframe into `alaska`'s CRS and verify the CRSs match using `assert`. ::: Let's check that map again: ::: {#2e87e551 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots() alaska.plot(ax=ax) places.plot(ax=ax, color='red', markersize=2) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=490 height=442} ::: ::: This is better: we can see the Alaska polygons and some of the `places` points on top of it. But why does the rest of the world look so strange? Every CRS is designed for an area of use (look for "Area of Use" in the output of `alaska.crs` above). EPSG:3338 is accurate around Alaska, so points far from Alaska get heavily distorted. We don't need them anyway: next, we'll keep only the points inside Alaska. ## Clipping **Clipping** means using a polygon (or polygons) to keep only the parts of the geometries that fall inside them. Clipping a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` is simple using the geopandas [`clip()` function](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/reference/api/geopandas.clip.html). The general syntax is: ```python updated_geodf = geopandas.clip(geodf, mask) ``` where: - `updated_geodf` is the output of the function: the intersection of the geometries in `geodf` with `mask`, - `geodf` is the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` we want to clip, - `mask` is a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` with the polygon(s) we want to use for clipping (we will see later that it can also be a bounding box). This `mask` must be in the same CRS as `geodf`! In our case: ::: {#26112344 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Clip populated places to Alaska multipolygon ak_places = gpd.clip(places, alaska) fig, ax = plt.subplots() alaska.plot(ax=ax) ak_places.plot(ax=ax, color='red') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=579 height=353} ::: ::: ## Prepare roads Now we move on to our roads dataset. ::: {#cffad5a3 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(roads.crs) roads.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EPSG:4326 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=202} ```{=html}

Before jumping right into reprojecting and clipping, we will subset the data to select only US roads: ::: {#74be2762 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} usa_roads = roads[roads['sov_a3'] == 'USA'] usa_roads.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=557 height=411} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution} ## Reduce your tabular data before reducing via geometries Geospatial operations are usually costly in terms of computing power. The more detailed our geometries are, the longer it takes to do geospatial computations. It's a good practice to reduce your data as much as possible before applying any geospatial transformation. ::: We will now compose functions to clip `usa_roads` using the `alaska` multipolygon. Notice we are using the output of `usa_roads.to_crs(alaska.crs)` directly and thus not changing the `usa_roads` geo-dataframe or creating new variables: ::: {#1809111d .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Clip usa_roads to alaska geometry ak_roads = gpd.clip(usa_roads.to_crs(alaska.crs), alaska) fig, ax = plt.subplots() alaska.plot(ax=ax) ak_roads.plot(ax=ax, color='red') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=579 height=353} ::: ::: Notice the short, disconnected segments in the southwest? Many of these "roads" are ferry routes that run over water. Clipping to the `alaska` polygons keeps only the pieces that cross land, so clipping *exactly* to the polygons isn't what we want here. ### Clipping with a bounding box We will clip the `usa_roads` geo-dataframe with the **bounding box** of `alaska` instead of its polygons. A bounding box is the smallest rectangle that contains all the geometries. It is defined by four coordinates, `minx, miny, maxx, maxy`: ![Image adapted from: National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON)](/book/images/lesson-13/bounding-box.png){width="80%"} Remember that the `total_bounds` attribute of a geo-dataframe gives us these four values: ::: {#83a841df .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} alaska.total_bounds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=206} ``` array([-2175729.73162241, 404545.10791528, 1493082.30904445, 2383808.43520816]) ``` ::: ::: `gpd.clip()` accepts these four values directly as the `mask`, so we can clip the roads to Alaska's bounding box in one step: ::: {#8641bd05 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} ak_complete_roads = gpd.clip(usa_roads.to_crs(alaska.crs), alaska.total_bounds) ``` ::: The bounds are just four numbers in the units of `alaska`'s CRS (meters, for EPSG:3338). They don't carry any CRS information, so it is up to us to make sure the data we clip is in the same CRS. Here, we do this by reprojecting `usa_roads` to `alaska.crs` before clipping. Notice the difference between the two clipping methods: ::: {#03dda229 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10,10)) ak_roads.plot(ax=ax1) ax1.set_title('Roads clipped with AK multipolygon') ak_complete_roads.plot(ax=ax2) ax2.set_title('Roads clipped with AK bounding box') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-22-output-1.png){width=495 height=818} ::: ::: How does this difference show up in the geo-dataframes themselves? Let's compare their number of rows and the total length of their roads. Since EPSG:3338 uses meters, the `length` attribute gives the length of each line in meters: ::: {#175f26bb .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('Number of roads (polygon clip):', len(ak_roads)) print('Number of roads (bbox clip): ', len(ak_complete_roads)) # Divide by 1000 to convert meters to kilometers print('Total length in km (polygon clip):', round(ak_roads.length.sum() / 1000)) print('Total length in km (bbox clip): ', round(ak_complete_roads.length.sum() / 1000)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of roads (polygon clip): 56 Number of roads (bbox clip): 56 Total length in km (polygon clip): 6069 Total length in km (bbox clip): 7111 ``` ::: ::: Both geo-dataframes have the same number of rows: clipping to the polygons did not drop any road. Instead, `gpd.clip()` *cut* the roads that cross the coastline, so the polygon clip has about 1,000 fewer kilometers of roads. The difference is in the geometries, not in the number of rows. (EPSG:3338 preserves areas, not distances, so these lengths are approximate, but they are good enough to compare the two results.) :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in `gpd.clip()` changed the geometries of the roads. What about their other columns? Compare the attributes of a few roads before clipping (in `usa_roads`) and after clipping (in `ak_roads`). What do you notice? ::: `gpd.clip()` only changes the geometries: all the other columns are copied unchanged from the original geo-dataframe. This means attributes that depend on the geometry, like the `length_km` column in our roads data, still describe the original, uncut features. If we need them for the clipped data, we have to recalculate them from the new geometries. ## Plot Finally, we can put all our data together in the same map: ::: {#ce5e334d .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11,5)) ax.axis('off') alaska.plot(ax=ax, color='whitesmoke', edgecolor='0.7') ak_complete_roads.plot(ax=ax, zorder=1, # Specify layer plotting order column='type', legend=True, legend_kwds={'title': "Road Types", 'loc': 'upper left', 'bbox_to_anchor':(0,0.9), 'fontsize':'small'} ) ak_places.plot(ax=ax, zorder=2, # Specify layer plotting order color='red', marker='s' # Square marker ) # Add city names as text annotations for x, y, name in zip(ak_places.geometry.x, ak_places.geometry.y, ak_places['name']): ax.text(x-30000, y+20000, name, fontsize=8, ha='right') ax.set_title("Roads, Ferry Routes and Selected Places in Alaska", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold') # Add data sources below the map ax.annotate("Data: Natural Earth (roads and populated places) and US Census Bureau TIGER/Line (state boundaries)", xy=(1, 0), xycoords='axes fraction', # Bottom-right corner of the axes ha='right', va='top', fontsize=8, color='gray') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-13-clipping_files/figure-html/cell-24-output-1.png){width=704 height=421} ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip} ## Exercise Notice the overlapping labels for Anchorage and Valdez: ![](/book/images/lesson-13/overlapping_points.png){width="40%" fig-align="center"} Update the map so these labels do not overlap. One way to do it is using an `if` when iterating over the Alaska populated places. Remember that the map is in the EPSG:3338 CRS, whose units are meters, so the label offsets (like `x-30000`) are in meters too. :::
